title: The charter
hook: the Medina charter makes the city's tribes, including its Jewish tribes, one community for defense

segments.voice: Yesterday: Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf turned down half his brother's wealth. Your line was: a trace of yellow perfume.

Clan after clan, written down one by one. That's how the document reads. Medina wasn't an empty town waiting for newcomers. It held Arab clans with old feuds between them, Jewish tribes with their own long histories there, and now emigrants from Mecca, far from home. Any of them could ask: whose city is this now? Who protects whom? Who pays when someone is hurt? The sirah of Ibn Ishaq preserves a written answer, drawn up under the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. Today: the charter.
screen: `CLAN AFTER CLAN.` → `OLD FEUDS, NEW ARRIVALS.` → `WHOSE CITY IS THIS NOW?`

segments.voice: As Ibn Ishaq gives it, the charter opens by naming the believers of Quraysh and of Yathrib, and those who join them and strive alongside them, and declares that they are one community, one ummah. Then it gets practical, clan by clan: each keeps its old customs for paying blood money and ransoming its captives, fairly and kindly. No one is to leave a debtor stranded. Then it turns to the Jewish tribes of the city. The Jews of the clan of Awf are named a community alongside the believers: to the Jews their religion, and to the believers theirs. Other Jewish clans are named in the same way. Each side bears its own expenses. They're to help one another against anyone who attacks the people of the document, and they owe one another sincere advice. And the valley of Yathrib is declared sacred for the people of the document. What kind of unity is this? It doesn't make everyone the same. Each clan keeps its customs; each religion keeps its own practice. It's a one made of many named parts, each listed, none erased. What binds them is a promise: to defend the city together, and to bring disputes to God and to Muhammad, not to the old feuds. Some historians ask how the text came together and when, and the city's later story has hard chapters ahead. But the document itself, as preserved, names party after party and gives each a place.
screen: `ONE UMMAH, NAMED CLAN BY CLAN.` · `EACH KEEPS ITS CUSTOMS.` · `TO THE JEWS THEIR RELIGION.` · `DEFEND THE CITY TOGETHER.` · then, large: `ONE COMMUNITY OF MANY.`

segments.voice: Think of a group you belong to where things are a little unclear or a little unfair: a household, a team, a shared apartment. In your mind, write it out like the charter, party by party, naming each person, giving each a fair part to carry, and letting each keep what matters to them. If you pray, you can ask Allah for fairness among you.

The charter. The agreement of Medina, preserved by Ibn Ishaq, that names the city's believers and its Jewish tribes, clan by clan, as one community for defense, each keeping its own religion. Today's word.
Your line: one community of many. A unity that didn't ask anyone to disappear. Day seven hundred seventy-four, done.

howItsDone: Muslims and historians study the charter of Medina (al-sahifah), preserved in Ibn Ishaq's sirah and other early works, and some Muslims point to it today when they speak of living alongside people of other faiths.

chat.says: Did the charter of Medina make everyone in the city follow one religion?
options: No. It named each group: to the Jews their religion, to the believers theirs.
Yes. Everyone in the city had to accept Islam to be protected.
No. It kept the groups fully apart, each owing the others nothing.
chat.meaning: As Ibn Ishaq gives it, each clan kept its customs and each religion its practice, and all were bound to defend the city together.

ummah.meaning: community; the word the charter uses for the people it binds

Awf.meaning: a clan of Medina whose Jews the charter names a community

Yathrib.meaning: Medina's older name, used in the charter

Ibn Ishaq.meaning: an early biographer of the Prophet who preserved the text

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the text of the charter of Medina: one ummah; clan customs of blood money and ransom; the Jews of Banu Awf a community with the believers, each with its religion; mutual defense; Yathrib sacred)

notes: All charter content is paraphrased from Ibn Ishaq's text as recalled; confirm each clause (one ummah; blood money and ransom by clan; debtor not left stranded; Jews of Banu Awf a community with the believers, 'to the Jews their religion and to the Muslims theirs'; each bears its own expenses; mutual defense; sincere advice; Yathrib sacred).
Abu Ubayd's Kitab al-Amwal as a second witness cited from memory; confirm.
Script avoids calling it 'the first constitution' or giving a date; scholars differ on dating and whether it is one document or several. Confirm framing.
The script mentions 'hard chapters ahead' without detail, to avoid framing the Jewish tribes as a foil. Confirm the later conflicts are handled with care on their own days.
'Disputes settled through agreed means': the charter refers disputes to Allah and Muhammad; confirm the softened paraphrase.
